localNote: St Mary Street, a few minutes north of Cardiff Central station, holds both the Prince of Wales and the Great Western, making them the easiest picks before a train or a match at the Principality Stadium. The Central Bar sits closer to Queen Street in the Windsor Place area, while the Mount Stuart is down in Cardiff Bay near the waterfront.

pubs.name: The Prince of Wales
pubs.history: Occupies a Victorian theatre opened in 1878 as the New Theatre Royal and renamed the Prince of Wales Theatre in 1920. It later served as a cinema and bingo hall before Wetherspoon restored it as a pub in 1999.
pubs.nearestStation: Cardiff Central, about 5 minutes on foot

pubs.name: The Central Bar
pubs.history: Takes its name from the Central Congregational Chapel, built on this Windsor Place site around 1901, at a time when Cardiff had dozens of nonconformist chapels.
pubs.nearestStation: Cardiff Queen Street, about 5 minutes on foot

pubs.name: The Great Western
pubs.history: Named after the Great Western Hotel, built around 1879 to serve travellers using the nearby Great Western Railway station, now Cardiff Central.
pubs.nearestStation: Cardiff Central, about 3 minutes on foot

pubs.name: The Mount Stuart
pubs.history: Housed in 1880s offices of the Mount Stuart Dry Docks Company, a name taken from the Marquesses of Bute's family seat on the Isle of Bute. It was a Harry Ramsden's restaurant before becoming a Wetherspoon in 2013.
pubs.nearestStation: Cardiff Bay, about 10 minutes on foot
